lines: In a software factory, verification is everything. <break time="0.4s" /> And for user interfaces, it's been the weakest link. <break time="0.4s" /> So... let's fix that, and then prove it actually works.

Here's the honest starting point. <break time="0.3s" /> The factory could already prove a screen had the right text and the right test ids, and that the tests passed. <break time="0.4s" /> But it couldn't tell you whether the screen actually looked right. <break time="0.3s" /> So, a person had to look. <break time="0.3s" /> And wherever verification stops... autonomy stops too.

So the idea is three layers. <break time="0.3s" /> First, measured. A script checks what can be measured, and gives the same answer every time. <break time="0.3s" /> Second, judged. A separate agent looks at the images, and has to cite evidence for every finding. <break time="0.3s" /> And third, accepted. A person sees the reference, the result, and the difference, side by side.

Here's how it fits into the pipeline. <break time="0.3s" /> A screenshot attached to the issue becomes the reference. <break time="0.2s" /> The visual spec turns it into a contract, and a person approves that, before anything is built. <break time="0.3s" /> The plan gives the page a visual gate. <break time="0.2s" /> The checker measures, and judges. <break time="0.2s" /> After the tests, the verifier runs again. <break time="0.3s" /> And when the person approves the result, those screens become baselines.

The measured layer is one small script. <break time="0.3s" /> It renders the screen in headless Chrome, then for each region in the contract, it checks five things. <break time="0.3s" /> Is it there. <break time="0.2s" /> Is it in the right place. <break time="0.2s" /> Does it say the right words. <break time="0.2s" /> Is it the right colour. <break time="0.2s" /> And does it look similar. <break time="0.4s" /> Every number goes into a report.
Now, here's the part most teams skip. <break time="0.4s" /> A verifier nobody has tested... is just an opinion. <break time="0.3s" /> So I tested it the way you'd test any other code.

I took a screen the factory had already built, and planted one defect at a time. <break time="0.3s" /> Like this one. The totals moved twenty-four pixels. <break time="0.3s" /> The region goes red on both sides, and the difference panel shows exactly what moved.
A swapped accent colour. <break time="0.3s" /> Caught by the colour check. The difference is measured, not eyeballed.
A table row that wraps onto two lines. <break time="0.3s" /> The box barely moved... but similarity caught it.

Six planted defects, and all six were caught. <break time="0.3s" /> And just as important, three harmless changes, like different sample data or a sub-pixel shift... and zero false alarms. <break time="0.3s" /> It runs in presubmit, so if anyone weakens the verifier, the build fails.
And it's deterministic. The same build, verified twice, gives a byte-for-byte identical report.
Okay. <break time="0.5s" /> Now, <break time="0.3s" /> let's run a real request through it... end to end.
The client attaches a screenshot to the issue, <break time="0.4s" /> and then writes what they want, <break time="0.2s" /> in plain words.
The intake saves that screenshot with the spec, <break time="0.2s" /> and the visual spec agent writes a contract from it.

And here's something I didn't plan for. <break time="0.4s" /> The first contract the agent wrote was wrong. <break time="0.3s" /> It measured the heading's text instead of the heading itself, and it demanded a total that only existed in the sample data. <break time="0.4s" /> Approve that, and a correct build would have failed three times.

So I didn't patch the contract. <break time="0.3s" /> I fixed the skill that writes contracts. <break time="0.3s" /> That's the meta loop, working. <break time="0.3s" /> And the second contract got it right.
The client approves the contract, along with the requirements, before a single line of code exists.
The plan gives the page section a fourth gate. <break time="0.2s" /> A visual check, against the reference.
And this is where it gets interesting. <break time="0.3s" /> The checker failed the page twice, <break time="0.2s" /> for two completely different reasons.
The first time, the measured layer caught it. <break time="0.3s" /> Names were wrapping, and the table was four hundred and sixty five pixels tall, against three hundred and twenty in the reference.

The second time... the verifier actually passed. <break time="0.3s" /> The maker had overcorrected. Tiny text, cramped rows. <break time="0.4s" /> The numbers squeaked through, but the checker's judgement didn't. <break time="0.3s" /> That's exactly why there are two layers.
On the third try, it passed. <break time="0.3s" /> Then the outer loop ran everything again. The evidence, the tests, <break time="0.2s" /> and the verifier, on its own.
Reference, built, and difference. <break time="0.3s" /> Every region green. <break time="0.3s" /> The only differences left are font rendering, because the runner draws text with Linux fonts.
And that image goes straight into the gate notice. <break time="0.3s" /> The person approving doesn't have to dig for anything.
Here's the dashboard, running.
And when it's approved, those screens become baselines. <break time="0.3s" /> The merge request carries them, so the next change to this screen gets checked against them, strictly.

Running it for real taught me three things. <break time="0.3s" /> A git quirk silently dropped the reference. The factory's own guardrail is what exposed it. <break time="0.3s" /> An agent's contract can be wrong, and that's exactly why a person approves it. <break time="0.3s" /> And a screenshot from one machine never matches pixels from another.

Now, the limits. <break time="0.3s" /> Boxes estimated from an image are approximate, so the tolerance is generous. <break time="0.3s" /> The judged layer is still a model's opinion, it's just forced to show its evidence. <break time="0.3s" /> And so far, it's been proven on one kind of screen.

Verification is what turns agents writing code into a factory you can trust. <break time="0.4s" /> The code is open source, and there's a test drive account if you want to look around. <break time="0.3s" /> Thanks for watching.
